table.title: [val] Co-bottleneck · Framework trade-offs
table.md:
| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Server rendering | Fast first paint, good for SEO, and simple caching at the CDN edge for anonymous pages. | Every interaction needs a round trip unless you add client code, and personalised pages are hard to cache. | Default |
| Static export | Cheapest to host and trivially scalable; pages survive backend outages. | Content updates need a rebuild, which gets slow once you have tens of thousands of pages. | Docs |
| Client SPA | Rich interactions and offline support once loaded. | Slow first load on mid-range phones, and search engines may index an empty shell. | Avoid |

conditions.browser: Chromium (Playwright build), macOS system fonts, deviceScaleFactor 1

candidates.name: d3r2B
candidates.idea: Test a compact scrolling layout with both prose columns above their longest-word widths. The shorter total scroll distance and narrower option column may improve access to weaknesses and verdicts, at the cost of taller rows.
candidates.label: gold

whys: The prose has the most natural line lengths and balanced row heights, with whole headers and words. The entire verdict column lies beyond the initial viewport, making recommendations less immediately discoverable.
The prose reads in more coherent phrases, with balanced rows and intact words. The initial viewport hides the entire verdict column, so readers must scroll to see the recommendation.
The prose reads in more natural phrases, with intact labels and a balanced distribution of space. The entire Verdict column is initially offscreen, which adds friction when comparing recommendations.

candidates.name: d3r3A

candidates.label: acceptable

whys: All columns and complete headers are visible at once, but rendering breaks inside the first option name. The narrow prose columns also produce long rows and short, fragmented lines.
All columns are visible and the headers stay whole, but ‘rendering’ breaks inside the word and the long prose forms tall, narrow blocks.
All four columns and intact headers fit in view, but ‘rendering’ splits across lines in the first option. The prose columns are narrow and rows are tall.

whys: All columns are visible and option names remain whole, but Verdict and Default split awkwardly. The prose columns remain narrow and the rows tall, weakening both lookup and continuous reading.
The option names remain whole, but both ‘Verdict’ and ‘Default’ split inside the word. The narrow prose columns also produce tall rows with considerable empty space beside them.
The option labels and prose fit without arbitrary word breaks, but the narrow final column splits both ‘Verdict’ and ‘Default’, damaging a key lookup column.

Headers and words remain whole, and the prose is more comfortable than in the tighter layouts. The verdict column is mostly offscreen initially, so checking recommendations requires a horizontal scroll.

candidates.name: contrast

Equal widths leave excessive room for Verdict while splitting both prose headers and words such as ‘interaction’ and ‘anonymous’. The long, narrow columns make comparison laborious.

Headers and words remain whole, and nearly the entire table is visible initially. The prose still wraps into very short lines and tall rows; the right edge of Verdict and Default requires a small scroll.
Words and headers remain whole, but the prose still occupies tall, narrow columns. A small scroll is needed to see the full verdict at the right edge.
Headers and words stay intact, with nearly the whole table visible initially. The prose remains tightly wrapped, and the right edge of Verdict and Default needs a small scroll.

d1.purpose: Compare three web rendering options and their trade-offs to support a choice.
tasks: Find an option and read its strengths, weaknesses and verdict across the row.
Compare strengths and weaknesses down their respective columns.
Scan verdicts, then read the supporting trade-offs before deciding.
Read each trade-off as a continuous sentence.
relations: Each row connects one option to its advantages, disadvantages and recommendation.
Strengths and weaknesses are paired explanations for the verdict.
Verdicts are short labels; their meaning depends on the trade-offs in the same row.
roles: Strengths and Weaknesses contain the main explanatory text and deserve most of the width.
Verdict is a compact decision aid.
The header labels the four distinct functions consistently across all rows.
keep_whole: Individual words, especially option names and column headers where space permits.
Short verdict labels and technical terms such as SEO, CDN and SPA.
may_wrap: Multiword option names may wrap between words.
Trade-off sentences may wrap naturally between words and at punctuation.
same_scale: Strengths and Weaknesses should have comparable widths because readers compare them, with some extra room for the longer weaknesses.
Option and Verdict are both identification aids, though Option needs more room for its longer labels.
d1.h_vs_v: A viewport-fitting table keeps every column visible but forces narrow prose, tall rows and some broken words. Scrolling allows natural wrapping and shorter rows, but readers must move horizontally to connect the option and verdict.

d2.purpose: Compare three rendering frameworks by their benefits, drawbacks and recommended use.
tasks: Find a framework and read its strengths, weaknesses and verdict across the row.
Compare the trade-offs and recommendations across frameworks.
relations: Strengths and weaknesses are paired explanations for the same option.
The verdict summarizes the practical recommendation for that option.
roles: Option identifies each row and anchors comparison.
Strengths and Weaknesses carry the longer explanatory prose.
Verdict is a short, high-value lookup field.
keep_whole: Individual words and verdict labels where space permits.
Framework names as recognizable phrases where practical.
may_wrap: Strengths and weaknesses prose at natural word boundaries.
same_scale: Strengths and Weaknesses should have comparable widths because they play parallel roles.
Option and Verdict can be narrower than the explanatory columns.
d2.h_vs_v: A viewport-fitting table exposes all four columns at once but forces narrow prose and some broken words; scrolling allows more natural reading at the cost of hiding columns initially.

d3.purpose: Compare three rendering approaches and their trade-offs to guide framework selection.
tasks: Find an option and read its strengths, weaknesses and verdict across the row.
Compare strengths, weaknesses and verdicts down their respective columns.
relations: Each row connects one option to its benefits, drawbacks and recommendation.
Strengths and weaknesses are parallel prose columns; the verdict summarizes the recommendation.
roles: The header row names the four comparison fields.
The first column identifies each option and acts as a row label.
The final column contains short verdicts.
keep_whole: Identifiers and abbreviations such as SEO, CDN and SPA
The option names where space permits
may_wrap: Strengths and weaknesses at natural word boundaries
Multiword option names between words when necessary
same_scale: Strengths and weaknesses should have comparable reading widths, with some extra space for the longer weaknesses.
Option and verdict columns can be narrower than the prose columns.
d3.h_vs_v: A viewport-width table avoids scrolling but forces very narrow prose columns, long rows and some broken words. Wider tables preserve words and improve prose reading at the cost of scrolling to see the verdict.

rounds.insights: The fitting layouts cannot accommodate all four columns at their measured unbreakable widths: those widths plus padding total 373 px. U makes the least disruptive overall compromise among the fitting examples, though its broken option name is conspicuous. S offers the strongest initial view among scrolling layouts because both trade-off columns are visible together; T and Q buy smoother prose and shorter rows at the cost of a viewport that cuts through Weaknesses. The best balance depends on whether seeing Verdict immediately matters more than uninterrupted prose.

analysis.strengths: All words and headers remain intact. The option names are easy to scan, and the two descriptive columns are visible on initial view.
analysis.faults: The first weakness wraps to nine lines, making the first row substantially taller than the others. The verdict column is entirely beyond the initial viewport.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrow weakness column controls row height while the shorter option and verdict cells leave considerable empty space.

analysis.strengths: All four columns, including verdicts, are visible at once. Headers stay on one line.
analysis.faults: The option “Server rendering” breaks inside “rendering.” Both prose columns are narrow, producing fragmented reading and a very tall table.
analysis.spatial_logic: Fitting the verdict into the viewport leaves too little width for the option names and descriptive text; the resulting height makes comparison across rows harder.

analysis.strengths: Words remain intact, and the wider weakness column makes the longest text notably easier to read. The first two rows have equal heights, giving the table a steadier rhythm than s0A.
analysis.faults: The verdict column is entirely outside the initial viewport. Strengths in the static export row wraps more tightly than in s0A, and the table still requires substantial vertical reading.
analysis.spatial_logic: Shifting width from strengths to weaknesses reduces the dominant first-row height. The option and both descriptive columns occupy the initial view, while verdicts require a horizontal scroll.

rounds.insights: S makes better use of roughly the same scrolling width as s0A: the weakness column is the stronger height bottleneck. A viewport-width table makes verdicts immediately available, but cannot accommodate every column's longest unbreakable unit at the stated padding and font size. The fitting class therefore needs a deliberate choice about where to accept a broken word.

bad.why: Both Weaknesses and Verdict break inside their headers, and several body words split. The narrow prose columns also make the table very tall.
Verdict and Default split inside words in the short lookup column, while the prose remains densely wrapped.

contrast.why: Equal columns fit the viewport but give the brief option and verdict fields space needed by the prose. Strengths and Weaknesses would break inside their headers and long words, producing a tall, difficult table.

sameFunctionGroups.why: Strengths and Weaknesses are parallel prose fields, so they should have comparable widths. Weaknesses can be somewhat wider because its content is longer.

synthesis.rationale: S is the strongest scrolling choice: it preserves words, gives both prose columns useful width, and shows the option and both trade-off columns at first sight. U is the best fitting candidate because it keeps all headers and verdicts visible, but its split in “rendering” is a real readability fault and makes it a conditional finalist. T and Q improve prose flow at the cost of showing less of Weaknesses initially; s0A needs similar scrolling to S but wraps the first weakness less naturally.

general: Protect whole words and clear headers before optimizing compactness.
Give parallel fields comparable visual weight while allowing their content to determine exact widths.
Judge a scrolling table by both its complete layout and the information visible at first sight.
specific: Reserve enough width for the short Verdict column to keep its header and values whole.
Give Weaknesses slightly more space than Strengths to accommodate its longer text.
At this viewport, showing all four columns forces an undesirable word break in the best fitting candidate.

synthesis.tradeoffs: S hides Verdict until the reader scrolls, whereas U exposes every column but splits an option name and produces long, narrow text blocks. T and Q reduce vertical reading effort but require more horizontal scrolling and initially show only part of Weaknesses.
synthesis.uncertain: U is the best of the supplied fitting layouts, not an unqualified publication choice; whether its broken option name is acceptable depends on how strongly avoiding horizontal scrolling is required. A fitting alternative with different widths has not been rendered or tested.

critique.cause: The 150 px and 170 px prose columns give comfortable reading measures but push the 73 px Verdict column beyond the viewport.

critique.good: Words and headers remain whole, and the small amount of scrolling exposes the rest of the table. The explanatory columns are balanced.
critique.problems: Prose remains very narrow and rows are almost as tall as in the fitting designs. The initial viewport cuts off part of the Verdict header and Default value despite the modest overflow.
critique.cause: The 110 px and 111 px prose columns are near their minimum whole-word widths; their combined width places the right edge of the 73 px Verdict column outside the viewport.

critique.good: All columns are visible, Weaknesses stays whole, and the slightly wider Weaknesses column gives some useful prose space.
critique.problems: The row anchor 'rendering', the Verdict header, and words in Strengths break awkwardly. The tall, uneven text blocks make scanning difficult.
critique.cause: The 78 px Option, 99 px Strengths and 71 px Verdict widths are too narrow for their longest relevant words.

critique.good: Headers and words stay whole, and the prose is substantially easier to read than in the near-fitting layouts. Its overflow is smaller than d2r4B's.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through Weaknesses and hides Verdict. Rows remain taller and prose more fragmented than in d2r4B.
critique.cause: The 140 px and 145 px prose widths are a compromise between reading measure and scrolling; together they still push Verdict off screen.

critique.good: All four fields are visible together, making it easy to locate an option and its verdict without scrolling. Option names wrap at word boundaries, and verdicts remain whole.
critique.problems: The weaknesses header and several prose words break inside words. The narrow prose produces tall rows and choppy reading, with large stretches of empty space in the option and verdict columns.
critique.cause: The 94 px strengths and 105 px weaknesses columns leave too little text width for their longest words and for comfortable phrases. The 87 px option and 73 px verdict columns leave little room to improve the prose within the viewport.

critique.good: Words and headers remain whole, prose wraps into manageable lines, and the two trade-off columns have comparable widths. The full table is reasonably compact and preserves clear row relationships.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the weaknesses column and hides the verdict, so reading a complete row requires horizontal scrolling. Server rendering wraps while the other option names fit on one line.
critique.cause: The 534 px table exceeds the viewport by 174 px; the 110 px option column is too narrow for Server rendering on one line.

critique.good: All option names and verdicts fit on one line, and the broad prose columns give natural, comfortable line breaks. The complete table has a calm, compact rhythm.
critique.problems: On a phone, the initial view cuts through strengths and shows neither weaknesses nor verdict. The long horizontal journey makes it harder to retain the option and compare a complete row, despite the attractive full render.
critique.cause: The 320 px and 350 px prose columns make the table 880 px wide, requiring 520 px of horizontal scrolling; the 136 px option column also consumes more of the initial viewport.

critique.good: All four fields and verdicts are visible without scrolling. Strengths and weaknesses have similar widths.
critique.problems: The weakness header, an option name and prose words break inside words. Tall rows and narrow fragments make comparison laborious, while the verdict cells contain large areas of unused vertical space.
critique.cause: The 80 px option and 105 px weakness columns are narrower than their longest unbreakable content; the 101 px strengths column is also too narrow for some words.

critique.good: All headers and words remain whole. The prose columns have comfortable, comparable widths, and the compact rows make comparisons easy in the full table.
critique.problems: The first viewport shows the option and strengths but only a sliver of weaknesses; the verdict requires substantial scrolling. The first two option names wrap.
critique.cause: The 200 px and 225 px prose columns produce a 599 px table; the 100 px option column cannot hold the longer names on one line.

critique.good: All four fields are visible without scrolling, and the option names wrap at word boundaries.
critique.problems: The weakness header and prose words split, and the tall rows leave verdict cells mostly empty. The narrower strengths column creates particularly fragmented reading.
critique.cause: The 87 px option column improves the row labels, but leaves only 94 px for strengths and 105 px for weaknesses.

critique.good: Headers and words remain whole. The option labels are clearer than in d3r1B, and the narrower table reduces the distance to the verdict while retaining readable prose.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through weaknesses and hides the verdict. Prose is more vertically fragmented than in d3r1B, producing taller rows.
critique.cause: The 165 px and 185 px prose columns balance reading width against scrolling, but the 534 px total still exceeds the viewport substantially.

critique.good: All four fields and verdicts are visible at once. The option names remain recognizable, and weaknesses has enough width for its header.
critique.problems: Strengths and Verdict break within their headers, and words such as anonymous and interactions split inside the prose. The long, narrow rows make comparison laborious and leave large empty areas under the short verdicts.
critique.cause: Strengths at 89 px and Verdict at 72 px are too narrow for their headers; the 89 px strengths column also forces word breaks. The 111 px weaknesses column takes a relatively large share of the constrained width.

critique.good: All headers and words remain whole. The first viewport shows the option and both prose columns almost completely, making the trade-offs easier to scan before scrolling.
critique.problems: The verdict is entirely beyond the initial viewport. Prose remains narrow and rows are tall, with several short lines and substantial blank space below option names and verdicts.
critique.cause: The 130 px and 145 px prose columns trade reading width for a relatively small 76 px scroll; the verdict starts just beyond the viewport.

critique.good: Option names fit on one line, prose reads comfortably, and the whole table has compact, clear rows with no broken words.
critique.problems: The first viewport shows only the beginning of weaknesses and hides the verdict, so comparing the two trade-off columns requires substantial horizontal movement. The wide option column consumes space that would help reveal more of the comparison.
critique.cause: The 136 px option column and 185 px strengths column place weaknesses near the right edge; the 600 px total requires 240 px of scrolling.

critique.good: All fields are visible without scrolling, and Strengths and Verdict stay on one line. Option names wrap at word boundaries.
critique.problems: Weaknesses breaks in its header, and words including anonymous, personalised and interactions break inside the prose. Tall rows and narrow lines make the table difficult to read continuously.
critique.cause: The 94 px strengths and 105 px weaknesses columns cannot accommodate all their words; 105 px is also insufficient for the Weaknesses header.

critique.good: The prose columns have comfortable, comparable widths, headers and words stay whole, and the table is considerably shorter than the fitting designs. Two option names fit on one line.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through the weaknesses column and hides the verdict. Server rendering wraps despite the extra option width, so that space does not keep every option name whole.
critique.cause: The 110 px option column falls short of the width needed for Server rendering, while the combined 165 px and 185 px prose columns push much of weaknesses beyond the viewport.

critique.good: All four fields and their headers are visible together, making row lookup and verdict comparison immediate. The prose columns have a sensible relative balance.
critique.problems: The first option breaks inside “rendering,” and the narrow prose columns produce long, fragmented rows with substantial empty space under the verdicts.
critique.cause: The 73px option column cannot contain “rendering”; the 102px and 111px prose columns leave little room for phrases.

critique.good: Words remain whole, prose reads in relatively natural phrases, and the shorter rows make comparison easier. The weaknesses have appropriately more room than the strengths.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the weaknesses and hides the verdict column, so reading a complete row requires horizontal movement.
critique.cause: The 155px and 170px prose columns improve reading but bring the table to 486px, 126px wider than the viewport.

critique.good: Words and headers remain whole, option names break naturally, and only a short horizontal scroll is needed to reach the verdicts.
critique.problems: The prose still reads in short fragments, producing tall rows. The initial viewport cuts through every verdict, obscuring the recommendations.
critique.cause: The 110px and 125px prose columns are only modestly wider than in the fitting layout; the verdict begins near the right edge of the viewport.

critique.good: The full table is visible at once, and the option names wrap between words.
critique.problems: Two headers split inside words, as do prose words. The resulting tall header and rows make the table harder to scan than d3r3A.
critique.cause: The 89px strengths column and 72px verdict column are too narrow for their headers; the strengths column also forces breaks inside body words.

critique.good: Words and headers remain whole. Both prose columns are readable in short phrases, and the first viewport shows the options and both prose columns together.
critique.problems: The verdicts are entirely offscreen initially. The strengths column still makes the second row particularly tall and leaves some uneven space beside shorter cells.
critique.cause: The 130px strengths column limits phrase length, while the 436px total width places the 73px verdict column beyond the viewport.

critique.good: All words and headers remain whole. The prose columns are comparable in scale, and option names wrap naturally. The table is shorter than the narrower alternatives.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through the weaknesses text and hides the verdict. Several prose passages still have short lines, and the first row is relatively tall.
critique.cause: The 145 px and 155 px prose columns preserve words but still require frequent wrapping; their combined width places the viewport edge inside the weaknesses column.

critique.good: Option names fit on one line, prose reads more continuously, and the table is the shortest shown. No words break internally.
critique.problems: The wide option column consumes space that would be useful for the comparison: the first viewport shows only a narrow slice of weaknesses and no verdict. The label column also leaves considerable empty space in the shorter rows.
critique.cause: The 136 px option column keeps the longest name whole but pushes the 170 px weaknesses column and verdict farther offscreen.

critique.good: All four fields are visible together, making the verdict easy to locate without scrolling. Headers and verdicts remain on one line.
critique.problems: The first option name breaks inside 'rendering'. Prose is fragmented into very short lines, producing tall rows and making comparisons harder to scan.
critique.cause: The 73 px option column is too narrow for its longest word, while the 102 px and 111 px prose columns leave little room beyond their longest unbreakable words.

critique.good: The first viewport shows the option and both prose columns nearly in full. Words remain whole, option names wrap naturally, and the verdict is only a short scroll away.
critique.problems: The strengths column produces several short lines and makes the second row especially tall. The verdict is outside the initial viewport.
critique.cause: The 130 px strengths column is narrow for continuous prose; the combined 362 px width of the first three columns places the verdict just beyond the viewport.

d2r0A.idea: Fit all columns within 359px, preserving the verdict while accepting dense rows and some split words.

d2r0B.idea: Use moderate horizontal scrolling to give the paired prose columns more room while keeping the overall table relatively compact.

d2r0C.idea: Use a wide scrolling table with a whole option column and generous prose columns for shorter, more continuous paragraphs.

d3r0A.idea: Fit the viewport, reserving room for verdicts while giving the remaining space to the two prose columns and accepting awkward breaks.

d3r0B.idea: Use moderate horizontal scrolling to keep words and headers intact while containing the table's width and height.

d3r0C.idea: Use generous scrolling widths to keep option names on one line and make the trade-off prose easier to read in short passages.

d1r0A.idea: Fit all four columns within 359px, preserving option words and verdicts while accepting cramped prose and some split words or headers.

d1r0B.idea: Use a compact scrolling table with readable word wrapping and moderately short rows, trading some horizontal movement for less vertical congestion.

d1r0C.idea: Give both trade-off columns broad reading measures and keep option names on one line, prioritizing continuous prose and comparison at the cost of substantially more horizontal scrolling.

d2r1A.idea: Test a fitting allocation that gives Option enough room for its longest word and Weaknesses enough for its header. Strengths becomes narrower, so inspect whether the remaining forced word breaks are an acceptable trade-off for seeing every column.

d2r1B.idea: Test a more compact scrolling layout. Keep framework words and verdicts whole while reducing the scroll distance and bringing more of Weaknesses into the initial viewport; check the resulting prose rhythm and row heights.

d2r1C.idea: Test an intermediate scrolling width with more comfortable prose than d2r0B and much less travel than d2r0C. Retain comparable explanation widths and allow multiword framework names to wrap.

d1r1A.idea: Test a viewport-fitting allocation that keeps the Weaknesses header whole while preserving option names and verdicts; check whether the narrower Strengths column causes unacceptable word breaks or height.

d1r1B.idea: Test a scrolling middle ground with more natural prose than B and less horizontal travel than C. Keep the option names wrapped at word boundaries and give Weaknesses slightly more room.

d3r1A.idea: Test a viewport-fitting redistribution that gives strengths enough width for its longest unbreakable unit while preserving the verdict and weaknesses widths. Option names may wrap more, and the weaknesses header and longest weakness word may still split; the render will show whether the trade improves reading.

d3r1B.idea: Test an intermediate scrolling layout with wider prose than d3r0B, giving weaknesses slightly more space while keeping the option column compact. This may reduce row height and improve phrase breaks without approaching d3r0C's scrolling distance.

d1r2A.idea: Test a fitting allocation that keeps both prose headers whole while preserving enough room for the longest option-name word and verdict labels. Prose will still be narrow, so inspect word breaks and row height.

d1r2B.idea: Test a middle-width scrolling layout. Reduce Option to the width already shown to hold its names, and give the recovered space to balanced prose columns while keeping the table narrower than d1r1B.

d1r2C.idea: Test a more compact scrolling layout that keeps words whole and brings more of Weaknesses into the initial viewport, while retaining more natural prose widths than either fitting design.

d2r2A.idea: Test a fitting compromise that preserves framework words and the Verdict header while giving Strengths more room than d2r1A. Weaknesses will still be forced to break its header or long words, an unavoidable trade-off at this width.

d2r2B.idea: Test a compact scrolling layout that keeps all headers and measured unbreakable words whole. Bringing more of Weaknesses into the initial viewport may improve the paired comparison, at the cost of taller rows than d2r1B.

d2r2C.idea: Test a middle ground between d2r1B and d2r0B: keep option words whole, give both prose columns more space than d2r1B, and reduce the scroll distance and initial concealment relative to d2r0B.

d3r2A.idea: Test a fitting layout that preserves whole option-name words and gives the weaknesses header and its longest word enough room. Strengths will still split some words; this tests whether concentrating the unavoidable damage in one prose column improves the result.

d3r2B.idea: Test a compact scrolling layout with both prose columns above their longest-word widths. The shorter total scroll distance and narrower option column may improve access to weaknesses and verdicts, at the cost of taller rows.

d3r2C.idea: Test a wider scrolling layout that keeps all option names on one line while retaining generous prose widths. This makes row identification more compact, with a similar total width to d3r1B.

d1r3A.idea: Test a fitting layout that preserves option names, both prose headers and long prose words by taking space from Verdict. Its header and Default will wrap within words, but the main explanatory text should read more continuously.

d1r3B.idea: Test a middle scrolling layout with more prose room than d1r2C and less horizontal travel than d1r2B. Keep the longer weaknesses slightly wider and retain whole headers and words.

d2r3A.idea: Test a fitting layout that gives Weaknesses enough room for its header while keeping the prose columns closer in scale than d2r1A. The narrower Option and Verdict columns may introduce breaks, so their rendering needs checking.

d2r3B.idea: Test a middle scrolling layout between d2r2B and d2r2C: give both prose columns more room than d2r2B while limiting the scroll distance and keeping the verdict closer to the initial viewport.

d3r3A.idea: Test a viewport-fitting allocation that gives both prose headers and Verdict enough width while keeping weaknesses wider. The narrower option column may break rendering; assess whether that localized cost improves the overall reading experience.

d3r3B.idea: Test a middle-width scrolling design: retain the compact option column, give both prose columns more room than d3r2B, and limit the total width to 485 px. This may reduce row height while keeping more of weaknesses visible initially than d3r0B.

d3r3C.idea: Test a compact scrolling design with enough room for the measured longest words and all headers. At 395 px total, it may expose part of the verdict initially while preserving whole words, though prose will remain narrow.

d2r4A.idea: Try a fitting compromise that keeps framework names intact and gives weaknesses enough room for its header, while preserving a full-width verdict; check whether the narrower strengths column produces unacceptable breaks.

d2r4B.idea: Explore a more spacious scrolling layout, giving the longer weaknesses prose extra width to reduce row height and improve continuous reading; assess the added horizontal travel.

d2r4C.idea: Try the narrowest practical scrolling layout with all long words and headers intact, keeping both explanatory columns comparable and reducing horizontal travel.

d1r4A.idea: Try a viewport-fitting compromise that keeps Verdict and its labels whole while giving both prose columns more room than d1r1A. The narrower Option column may split its longest name component, so check that trade-off in the render.

d1r4B.idea: Try a more compact scrolling layout with both prose columns above their longest-word minimums. It should expose more of Weaknesses initially and reduce travel to Verdict, at the cost of taller rows.

d1r4C.idea: Test a wider reading-oriented scrolling layout with comparable prose columns and extra room for the longer weaknesses. Check whether shorter, more continuous sentences justify the additional horizontal travel.

d3r4A.idea: Test a middle ground between d3r2B and d3r3B: give both prose columns more room while keeping the total width and scrolling below d3r3B.

d3r4B.idea: Test keeping every option name on one line alongside the more readable prose widths of d3r3B. This costs additional scrolling but may improve row identification and comparison.

d2r5A.idea: Try a fitting layout that preserves framework names, verdicts and the Strengths header. Concentrate the unavoidable prose and header breaks in Weaknesses, then assess whether the cleaner row anchors and verdict improve scanning.

d2r5B.idea: Test a moderate-scroll layout between d2r4C and d2r3B. Give both prose columns more room while keeping overflow lower than d2r3B.

d2r5C.idea: Test a more generous scrolling layout for continuous prose reading and shorter rows, with slightly more width for the longer Weaknesses content.

d1r5A.idea: Try a fitting layout that keeps option names and verdicts whole. It trades some prose and header integrity for an intact decision aid; compare its actual breaks with d1r3A.

d1r5B.idea: Test a compact scrolling layout with enough space for the longest words and headers. Its 408 px total should reduce horizontal travel while improving on the fitting layouts' broken words.

d1r5C.idea: Test an intermediate scrolling layout between d1r4B and d1r2B, seeking more comfortable prose with a 490 px total and less horizontal movement than d1r2B.

d3r5A.idea: Keep option names at natural two-line breaks while giving both prose columns the widths used in d3r4B. Test whether its shorter rows justify the additional scrolling compared with d3r2B.

d3r5B.idea: Test a viewport-width alternative that gives the option column enough space for 'rendering' and preserves the prose columns' longest words. The narrower verdict column may force a header or verdict break; check whether that trade-off improves the overall fit.

s0A.idea: Keep the option names and verdict intact while placing the end of Weaknesses at the viewport edge. Compared with S, shift some prose width to Strengths, which wraps heavily in the static-export row. Check the rendered line breaks and row heights.

s0B.idea: Offer a roomier scrolling alternative between T and Q. Give both prose columns more space than T while limiting the extra scroll, then check whether the resulting line breaks justify the added width.

s1A.idea: Keep option names intact in a viewport-fitting layout and distribute the remaining width between the prose columns. Check where unavoidable word breaks fall and whether the verdict remains easy to scan.

s1B.idea: Test a fitting alternative that preserves more space for strengths while keeping option names intact; compare its weakness breaks and row heights with the first refinement.

s1C.idea: Build on S by giving strengths a little more room while retaining its effective weakness width. Check whether the extra scroll buys more natural wrapping or shorter rows.

contrast.idea: Equal columns fit the viewport but give the brief option and verdict fields space needed by the prose. Strengths and Weaknesses would break inside their headers and long words, producing a tall, difficult table.

d2r4A.why: Everything is visible, but Weaknesses and Verdict split in their headers, and words such as anonymous and interactions break across lines. Narrow text columns make the rows long and difficult to scan.

vc_pref.why: Headers and words remain whole, and the prose is more comfortable than in the tighter layouts. The verdict column is mostly offscreen initially, so checking recommendations requires a horizontal scroll.

ref_auto.why: Headers and words remain whole, and nearly the entire table is visible initially. The prose still wraps into very short lines and tall rows; the right edge of Verdict and Default requires a small scroll.

d3r2B.why: The prose has the most natural line lengths and balanced row heights, with whole headers and words. The entire verdict column lies beyond the initial viewport, making recommendations less immediately discoverable.

d3r3A.why: All columns and complete headers are visible at once, but rendering breaks inside the first option name. The narrow prose columns also produce long rows and short, fragmented lines.

d1r3A.why: All columns are visible and option names remain whole, but Verdict and Default split awkwardly. The prose columns remain narrow and the rows tall, weakening both lookup and continuous reading.

ref_auto.why: Words and headers remain whole, but the prose still occupies tall, narrow columns. A small scroll is needed to see the full verdict at the right edge.

d3r2B.why: The prose reads in more coherent phrases, with balanced rows and intact words. The initial viewport hides the entire verdict column, so readers must scroll to see the recommendation.

variants.why: critical point of the most fragile column

ratings.why: The first option splits 'rendering' before its final letter, while the strengths and weaknesses remain as tall as in G. The verdict also requires scrolling.
The first option breaks 'rendering' into 'renderin / g', damaging a key lookup label. The prose columns otherwise have the same useful balance as A, with verdicts off-screen.
The strengths column is easier to read, but the narrower weaknesses column leaves 'and' alone in the first row and increases its height. The verdict requires scrolling.
The wider strengths column improves the second row, but the first weakness grows to eight lines with a stranded 'and'. All words remain whole, while the verdict column remains off-screen.
Words stay whole and strengths read comfortably, but the cramped weaknesses column makes the first two rows very tall and leaves conspicuous empty space beside them.

Strengths read more smoothly and words stay whole, but weaknesses become very narrow and extend to nine lines. The resulting tall rows and large empty areas make comparison slower; verdicts remain off-screen.
All words remain whole, but the weakness text wraps more tightly than in G, including 'tens of / thousands of / pages'. The verdict is beyond the initial viewport.

All words remain whole, but the narrower weaknesses column creates more fragmented phrases, including 'tens of / thousands of / pages.' Extra verdict width does little for its short entries, which remain off-screen.
The verdict column splits both its header and 'Default' inside words. The taller header and broken decision label undermine scanning, despite the more generous weaknesses column.

The wider weaknesses column improves some phrases, but 'Verdict' and 'Default' both split inside the word. The broken header also makes the header row taller, and the verdict column remains off-screen.
The wider strengths column reduces wrapping, but 'rendering' breaks before its final letter in the first option, damaging a key lookup label.
The wider strengths column gives the second row more natural phrases and a shorter row, but the first option breaks 'rendering' before its final letter. Verdicts remain off-screen.
Client SPA fits on one line and weaknesses wrap naturally, but the extra option width makes strengths more fragmented than in C. The verdict column is offscreen initially.
The option labels are easy to scan and weaknesses read naturally, though strengths wrap more tightly than in A. The verdict requires scrolling.
Weaknesses read in relatively comfortable lines, but strengths become narrow and the first strength stretches to nine lines. The resulting imbalance leaves considerable empty space beside it.
Weaknesses read in relatively coherent phrases, but the first strength is fragmented across nine lines and leaves uneven space beside it. The verdict requires scrolling.
Strengths have useful width and all words stay whole, but the first weakness stretches to nine lines, including an isolated 'and'. The verdict column is offscreen initially.
Strengths read more comfortably, but the first weakness is broken into nine short lines, including a line containing only 'and'. The verdict requires scrolling.
Words remain intact, but the first weakness runs to nine short lines. The verdict column has more width than its content needs, while only fragments of it appear initially.
The first weakness runs to nine lines while the verdict column has unused width. A sliver of the verdict appears at the viewport edge, but reading it requires scrolling.
The verdict header and all three verdicts break inside words, making the column hard to scan. The wider weaknesses column reads better, but its right edge and the verdict require scrolling.
The verdict header and every verdict break inside words. The wider weakness column also extends beyond the initial viewport, so some lines require scrolling to finish.
The option header and key option names split inside words, including 'Server rendering' across four fragments. This damages the primary lookup column despite the more readable strengths text.
The narrow option column breaks its header and row labels inside words, making the entries harder to identify. The descriptive columns are more comfortable, but the verdict remains offscreen.
Some option names fit on one line, but the narrow strengths column produces a nine-line first cell and a tall, uneven table. Verdicts remain offscreen initially.
Two option labels fit on one line, but the narrow strengths column produces choppy passages and tall rows. The verdict is entirely beyond the initial viewport.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement (one model, independent fresh contexts); not cross-model validation, not human preference or reading data
